The firing of George Perlegos as chairman and chief executive of Atmel Corp. is an unusual case in that the man legally retaliated against those who coördinated the decision. Membership in the board of directors of Atmel Corp. used to be exclusively held by insiders, until a N.A.S.D.A.Q. rule requiring a majority of directors to be independent came into being. The five independent directors fired George & Gust Perlegos and two other executives on 7 Aug. 2006 in a board vote. George Perlegos claimed that a special shareholders' meeting was called before he was terminated; the result of the purported conference was that the five independent directors were themselves removed from office. Not surprisingly, the five independent directors disputed the allegation that such a convening occurred before George Perlegos was forced to quit. The five independent directors articulated the reasons behind George Perlegos's termination in a letter addressed to him as being "...based on your conduct in regard to personal and family air travel at company expense, and the lack of controls for preventing misuse of company resources." On 25 July 2001, the company launched an investigation into stock option grants' timings for the executives. What was not publicized was that a secret investigation to which only the independent directors were privy to was reviewed a few days before the announcement. This investigation concluded in Nov. 2005 that George Perlegos siphoned off $326K from corporate coffers in paying 338 air-line tickets for himself and his family. Gust Perlegos, who was the executive vice-president of Atmel Corp., was found separately to have misappropriated $80K in company funds to purchase 146 air-line tickets for his family and himself. Notably, the two investigations were not officially tied together by the company. The Perlegoses responded by filing three disparate suits in law against Atmel Corp. in Delaware state court, battles which were still raging at the time of publication of the cited New York Times article. The absence of a formal employment agreement meant the directors were within their rights to fire the Perlegoses, but George Perlegos countered that the travel cost violations were perpetrated by a terminated employee. Therefore, he argued that the independent directors went out of line in their fiduciarial capacities. The article reported, “'The hasty, secretive and precipitous manner in which they have purported to act,' said a suit the brothers filed, 'will have devastating consequences for the company, including but not limited to the loss of the Perlegoses’ decades of experience in running the company and a significant loss of shareholder value.'" Auditors accepted management's claims of solid internal controls in an annual report of the previous year, but Atmel Corp. had been in the red for years. The stock quote inched upwards to $5 from $2 at the same time in the previous year, yet it was a far cry from the $30.69 level in 2000. A departure code of "4" has been tentatively assigned to the case in light of the information gathered from the article.
